explanations.explanation: Dwelling place is it. Moses, Israel's leader, says “…You have been our dwelling place through all generations.” That's a home, and not just for one family but for everybody down the line. I once lived in a junk drawer, and nobody would call that a dwelling place with a straight face.

A shield is a fine picture, but it's not the one Moses uses here. He says the Lord has been “our dwelling place through all generations.” A shield is something you pick up when trouble comes. A dwelling place is where you live every single day, and I think that's a warmer thing to say about Him.

Shepherd is a lovely word, friend, but it's not the one in this verse. Moses says “…our dwelling place through all generations.” So the picture is a home, with a door that stays open for the whole family line. Keep the shepherd in your pocket, because this psalm is going to move in a different direction.

True! The psalm says, “…from everlasting to everlasting You are God.” That covers the time before the mountains were born, and before He brought forth the earth and the world. There's no starting line on this one, friend. I can barely remember where I put my own apron.

This one's true, friend, so False tripped you up. The psalm says, “…from everlasting to everlasting You are God.” That's before the mountains were born and before He brought forth the earth and the world. Nothing in this verse puts an edge on it.
Dust! The verse says, “You return man to dust…” It's a plain, quiet line, and it sets up the picture of how short our days are. We'll watch the psalm keep building on that.

Youth sounds like a happy ending, I'll give you that. But the verse says, “You return man to dust…” So the psalm is being plain with us about how short life is. The good news is that the psalm doesn't stop there.

Glory is a big, shiny word, but it's not the one in this verse. The text says, “You return man to dust…” It's much simpler than glory. Same dust that gets on my counter after a long day of baking, only a lot more serious.

A day gone by. The psalm says a thousand years in His sight “…are but a day that passes, or a watch of the night.” That's a thousand years squeezed into one day. Meanwhile I get impatient when my first batch takes twelve minutes.

A lifetime is a long stretch, friend, but the verse shrinks it further. The psalm says a thousand years in His sight “…are but a day that passes, or a watch of the night.” So it's a day, not a lifetime. I think that's the point of the picture: time looks very different from where He stands.

That's the opposite direction, friend. The verse doesn't stretch a thousand years out, it shrinks it down. A thousand years in His sight “…are but a day that passes, or a watch of the night.” A big number goes in and a small one comes out.
New grass! The psalm says people are “…like the new grass of the morning.” It's fresh and green at sunrise, and that's the picture Moses picks. Next verse, we find out what happens to it.

A cedar is a big tree, but that's not Moses' picture. He says people are “…like the new grass of the morning.” Grass is small, soft and new. I think he picked something that looks fresh and fragile on purpose.
A fig tree is a good guess, but it's not in this psalm. The text says people are “…like the new grass of the morning.” So the picture is grass, not a tree. And grass has a very short schedule.

Evening. The psalm says, “…in the morning it springs up new, but by evening it fades and withers.” The whole story fits inside one day. Up at sunrise and done by supper time, and I think that's exactly what Moses wants us to see.

Winter would give the grass a whole season, and this grass doesn't get one. The verse says, “…in the morning it springs up new, but by evening it fades and withers.” It's one day, friend. Morning to evening.

Harvest is a good word, but it's not in this verse. The text says, “…in the morning it springs up new, but by evening it fades and withers.” So the clock here is morning and evening, nothing longer. It's a quick picture on purpose.

Our secret sins. The verse says, “You have set our iniquities before You, our secret sins in the light of Your presence.” Nothing is tucked away from Him. I think this one is heavy, friend, so it's okay to just sit with it a moment.

Good deeds aren't what Moses names here. He says, “You have set our iniquities before You, our secret sins in the light of Your presence.” This is a heavy verse, and it's about what's hidden coming into the light. I think Moses wants us to take it seriously.

Offerings aren't what this verse is about. It says, “You have set our iniquities before You, our secret sins in the light of Your presence.” It's a heavy line, so I won't joke about it. The things we keep hidden are set in the light of His presence.

Seventy, or eighty if we're strong. That's how the verse puts it: “The length of our days is seventy years—or eighty if we are strong…” It's a short window, friend. I'll say this: I've spent a chunk of mine in a drawer, so I take that number seriously.

Nine hundred is a very long time, but that's not the number here. The verse says, “The length of our days is seventy years—or eighty if we are strong…” So Moses is talking about a much shorter stretch. Nine hundred years would need a LOT of birthday cookies.

That's a big number, but it's not the one Moses uses. The verse says, “The length of our days is seventy years—or eighty if we are strong…” So he gives us seventy, with eighty as the strong version. It's a short stretch on purpose.
It's the other way around, friend. The verse says they “…quickly pass, and we fly away.” So those years don't drag, they zip by. Quick, just like that.
False is right. The psalm says those years “…quickly pass, and we fly away.” Fast, not slow. I used to think a drawer made time crawl, but Moses says life is quick.
True. The psalm says, “Your wrath matches the fear You are due.” It's a heavy line, and I think Moses means it to be. We've been in some serious verses, friend, and the prayer is about to turn.
This one's true, friend. The verse says, “Your wrath matches the fear You are due.” It's a heavy line, so I won't joke about it. I'd say Moses means for it to be heavy.

explanations.answer: To present a heart of wisdom
explanations.explanation: A heart of wisdom! The prayer says, “So teach us to number our days, that we may present a heart of wisdom.” He doesn't ask to number days just to count them. The reason he gives is wisdom. That's a better reason than mine for counting dust.

Storehouses would be a practical reason, but Moses doesn't give it. The prayer says, “So teach us to number our days, that we may present a heart of wisdom.” His reason is a heart of wisdom, not a full pantry. Wisdom is the point of the whole request.

Nobody's outlasting anybody in this verse, friend. Moses says, “So teach us to number our days, that we may present a heart of wisdom.” The reason is wisdom, and enemies don't come into it. It's a quiet request, not a competition.
True. Moses prays, “Return, O LORD! How long will it be? Have compassion on Your servants.” After all those heavy verses, he asks for compassion. I think that's a good move.
That one's true, friend. Moses prays, “Return, O LORD! How long will it be? Have compassion on Your servants.” So compassion is exactly what he asks for. The prayer is turning toward hope.

His loving devotion! The prayer says, “Satisfy us in the morning with Your loving devotion…” That's what he asks for to start the day. Good thing too, because I'm not satisfied before my first batch of cookies.

Mighty power is a big request, but it's not the one here. The prayer says, “Satisfy us in the morning with Your loving devotion…” So it's loving devotion that fills the morning. Fits right in with how the prayer is warming up.
The law isn't what he asks for in this verse. The prayer says, “Satisfy us in the morning with Your loving devotion…” It's loving devotion that satisfies. That's a gentle way to start a morning.
It's bigger than one day, friend. The prayer says, “…that we may sing for joy and be glad all our days.” All our days, not just one. Moses asks for a lot of gladness.
False is right. Moses asks God to satisfy them “…that we may sing for joy and be glad all our days.” That's every day, not just one. I'd take that over a single good day any time.

Afflicted. The prayer says, “Make us glad for as many days as You have afflicted us, for as many years as we have seen evil.” Moses is asking for gladness to match the hard days. It's a very honest prayer.

Blessed sounds nice, but the verse uses a harder word. It says, “Make us glad for as many days as You have afflicted us…” So Moses asks for gladness to match the hard days. That's an honest thing to pray.

Taught is a good guess, since verse 12 had him asking to be taught. But this verse says, “Make us glad for as many days as You have afflicted us…” So it's about the hard days, and gladness to match them. It's a very real prayer.

Their children. The prayer says, “May Your work be shown to Your servants, and Your splendor to their children.” Moses is looking past his own generation. That's the same family line the psalm began with.

The nations aren't named in this verse. The prayer says, “May Your work be shown to Your servants, and Your splendor to their children.” So it's the servants' children Moses has in mind. He's thinking about the next generation.

Kings don't show up in this verse. The prayer says, “May Your work be shown to Your servants, and Your splendor to their children.” So it's the children he asks about, not the kings. It's a family-sized request.
The work of their hands! The prayer ends, “…establish for us the work of our hands—yes, establish the work of our hands!” He asks it twice, friend. I'd say that's the part he really means.

City walls aren't in this verse. The prayer ends, “…establish for us the work of our hands—yes, establish the work of our hands!” It's the work of their hands, and he says it twice. Everyday work, said with all his heart.

A throne isn't what Moses asks about here. The prayer ends, “…establish for us the work of our hands—yes, establish the work of our hands!” He asks about the work of their hands, and he says it twice. It's a plain request, and I think he means it with his whole heart.
